claims.text: Residual internal stresses are concentrated at grain boundaries and microstructural defects in as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloys.
Residual internal stresses govern the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of these alloys.
Residual stresses mediate magnetostructural coupling during low-applied-field cycles.
Residual stresses locally enhance the first-order magnetostructural transition.
Controlled stress relaxation will broaden the magnetostructural transition.
Controlled stress relaxation will reduce hysteresis.
The as-deposited films have a predominant ordered single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited films have a fine microstructure with a high density of grain boundaries.
Low-temperature inert-atmosphere annealing can relax residual stresses without causing significant grain growth or phase decomposition.
Residual internal stresses enhance local magnetoelastic coupling.
Enhanced local magnetoelastic coupling sharpens the magnetostructural transition.
A sharper magnetostructural transition contributes to a large but hysteretic entropy change.
Annealing reduces hysteresis by mitigating abrupt domain reconfigurations and phase-boundary pinning.
Post-annealed samples will have a broader magnetostructural transition than the as-deposited baseline.
Post-annealed samples will have lower hysteretic losses than the as-deposited baseline.
Post-annealed samples will exhibit a more gradual entropy change during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
The as-deposited alloy exhibits a sharp, hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transition with a large entropy change.
The predictions apply within the non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi composition range in which the ordered hexagonal phase remains stable.
Phase transformations or significant microstructural coarsening would place the annealed material outside the proposed prediction boundary.
